strengths: The paper contributes a useful NLP resource: 20,281 preference pairs derived from naturally occurring conversational feedback, with both GPT-4 and policy-model generation variants. Retaining feedback-derived preference descriptions makes the dataset valuable beyond standard preference training.

Downstream results support the dataset’s practical utility across three model families and three public benchmarks. For example, Qwen 2 trained on WF On-policy improves AlpacaEval’s length-controlled win rate from 28.7% to 42.6% and Arena-Hard performance from 24.9% to 36.1%. These results provide evidence beyond the proposed checklist metric.

The experiments include regenerated UltraFeedback controls, length-controlled evaluation, and a reported conversation- and user-disjoint test set. Human validation covers feedback identification in 50 conversations and checklist evaluation in 200 conversations, providing useful checks on automated annotation.

The pipeline is clearly explained, with detailed prompts, rubrics, model identifiers, and principal SFT/DPO hyperparameters. The dataset release and cross-model results support a contribution suitable for Findings, although the broader alignment claims need stronger evidence.
weaknesses: Improved alignment with actual users and reduced evaluator bias are not established directly. GPT-4 extracts preferences, generates or filters training pairs, and evaluates responses using similarly constructed checklists. Appendix C reports 57.14% agreement with humans and kappa 0.372, but does not show that checklists improve human agreement relative to evaluation without them. Increased checklist scores therefore provide limited independent validation of the central alignment claim.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution of natural feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, filtering, and dataset size. A control using the same WildChat prompts without feedback guidance, alongside an SFT-only ablation, would help distinguish feedback-specific benefits from domain adaptation and improved supervised targets.

The custom test set deliberately selects central preferences within 70 clusters. This is defensible for studying common preferences, but does not establish population representativeness or coverage of diverse user needs. The feedback detector’s 48.4% DSAT recall also suggests substantial omissions whose distribution is unexplored. The acknowledged selection bias consequently remains important to interpreting generalization.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority over UltraFeedback overstate Table 3. For Qwen 2 with GPT-4-generated data, WildFeedback scores below UltraFeedback on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Several positive margins elsewhere are small, and no confidence intervals or variation across training runs are reported.

Although the core training recipe is documented, exact reproduction would benefit from generation sampling settings, the embedding model and precise clustering/deduplication procedure for test selection, the method used to identify disjoint users, and the validation criterion used during hyperparameter search. These details particularly matter because data construction and evaluation-set selection are central contributions.
